sections.title: 1. Parental Mental Illness, Childhood Adversity & Abuse

blocks.text: Rutter's model of how parental psychiatric disorder affects a child: (1) direct pernicious impact of exposure to the parental disorder, (2) indirect impact via altered interpersonal behaviour/parenting capacity, (3) mediator variables such as social adversity or genetic/constitutional factors (Murray & Cooper, 1997).

Maternal depression's effects change by developmental stage: prenatal (poor nutrition, preterm birth, low birth weight, pre-eclampsia); infant (anger/protective coping, passivity, reduced attention/**IQ**); toddler (passive noncompliance, reduced autonomy, internalizing/externalizing problems); school-age (reduced adaptive functioning, affective/anxiety/conduct disorders, **ADHD**-like presentation); adolescent (affective, anxiety, conduct disorders, substance/alcohol dependence).

**WHO** World Mental Health Survey Initiative (Kessler 2010, 21 countries): parental death is the most common childhood adversity (11.0–14.8%); physical abuse 5.3–10.8%; family violence 4.2–7.8%; parental mental illness 5.3–6.7%. Adversities linked to maladaptive family functioning raise adult psychiatric disorder risk with **OR** 1.3–2.4; other adversity types carry a lower, often nonsignificant risk. Findings were consistent globally.

Of reported child maltreatment cases, approximately 60% are neglect, 20% physical abuse, 10% sexual abuse, and 10% other (e.g. psychological abuse, abandonment). Sexual abuse: girls are victims 4:1 over boys, 90% of abusers are male, average age 9–11 years. Most common sexual-abuse relationship is stepfather–stepdaughter.

Physical abuse risk factors: poverty/financial stress, less parental education, underemployment, single parenting, multiproblem families (domestic violence, social isolation, parental mental illness/alcoholism), young/low-**IQ**/criminal-record parents, and child factors (prematurity, congenital malformation, intellectual disability, difficult temperament). Sexual abuse: socioeconomic status is unrelated to incidence (though lower classes are more likely to come to attention); associated with alcohol abuse, overcrowding, rural isolation.

Sexually abused children show higher morning cortisol levels than non-abused children. Factitious disorder/Munchausen's syndrome by proxy (a person feigning/inducing illness in a child) is a recognised form of child abuse, hard to detect as the perpetrator may deny or cover up.

Child-abuse-signs **EMI**: 'stained underwear / discomfort walking or sitting' maps to **SEXUAL** abuse, 'poor personal hygiene / untreated medical problems' maps to physical **NEGLECT**, and 'sudden speech disorder / rocking / head-banging' maps to **EMOTIONAL** abuse — these overlapping physical/behavioural sign lists across abuse subtypes are a classic **EMI** cross-matching trap.

blocks.text: **DSM-5** changes to **ADHD**: onset criterion changed from 'symptoms causing impairment before age 7' to 'several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms present prior to age 12'; subtypes replaced by presentation specifiers; comorbid diagnosis with autism spectrum disorder is now allowed; adult symptom threshold lowered to 5 symptoms (vs 6 for younger persons) for both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity.

Prevalence: **DSM-IV** criteria give ~5% in school-age children generally, 3–4% in **UK** children; **ICD-10** criteria give ~1–2%. **ADHD** is 3x more prevalent in boys, and more common in social deprivation and institutional care.

Genetics: heritability ~80%; siblings have 2–3x increased risk; **MZ** twin concordance 79% vs **DZ** 32%. Associated with the dopamine transporter gene (**DAT1**) and dopamine **D4** receptor gene; **SNAP-25** gene may also have a role. Genes 5, 6 and 11 implicated.

Neuroimaging/neurotransmitters: prefrontal cortex, striatum and cerebellum affected; **PET** shows lower cerebral blood flow/metabolic rate in frontal areas, and adolescent females with **ADHD** show globally lower glucose metabolism than controls and than affected males. **DA**/**NA** dysregulation in the prefrontal cortex is implicated (not primarily serotonin).

Environmental factors with an evidence base: prenatal/perinatal obstetric complications, low birth weight/prematurity, prenatal alcohol/nicotine/benzodiazepine exposure, poor attachment/severe early deprivation, institutional rearing. Idiosyncratic reactions to food/additives and lead exposure are **NOT** supported by research evidence. Head injury before age 2 is not shown to be causal (**BMJ** retrospective cohort) — it may instead be a 'marker' for later **ADHD** diagnosis.

Comorbidity (50–80% have ≥1 comorbid disorder; 50% meet criteria for 2): oppositional defiant disorder 40%, anxiety disorder 34%, conduct disorder 14%, tics 11%, mood disorder 6% (Young et al 2011, **BMC** Psychiatry).

Outcome: ~15% still meet full **ADHD** criteria at age 25; a further ~50% have residual impairment. 5x greater risk of antisocial behaviour/substance misuse/other psychiatric disorders; 15–20% develop substance misuse. Combined-type presentations tend to show fewer hyperactive-impulsive symptoms with age, evolving toward inattentive-type presentation. Poor prognosis: early stressful life experiences, severe/predominantly hyperactive-impulsive symptoms, and comorbid conduct/language/learning disorder.

**ADHD** has the highest heritability among common childhood psychiatric conditions (70–80%); risk in siblings is 2–3x increased. Rates are also increased in extreme prematurity, prenatal tobacco/alcohol exposure, and after head injury, though none of these prenatal factors is confirmed as causal.

blocks.text: Management principle: try psychological/social interventions before medication — educational/remedial interventions, parent training (social learning theory/behavioural), individual/family/group therapies, **CBT** (especially behavioural), social skills training.

**MTA** study (largest **RCT**, n=579): confirmed medication management's effectiveness; intensive behavioural therapy added little to well-supervised medication management, though psychological interventions matter for families declining medication. Evidence for efficacy over prolonged treatment periods is lacking.

**Methylphenidate**: fastest onset (1–3h) and shortest half-life (2–3h) of the stimulants, so effects wear off in 4–6h; dose range 5–60mg/day, titrated in 5–10mg weekly increments. Growth retardation may occur acutely but not significantly long-term. Stimulant prescribing does **NOT** increase later substance-abuse rates. Pemoline is no longer licensed in the **UK** (abnormal LFTs, rare liver failure).

**Atomoxetine** (noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor): doesn't affect dopamine, so doesn't worsen tics. **MHRA** (Dec 2012): can cause clinically relevant **BP**/heart-rate increases — monitor; also monitor for depression/suicidality. Rarely causes liver damage, so routine **LFT** monitoring is **NOT** warranted.
Monitoring: height, weight, **BP** and heart rate for **methylphenidate** (initially 3-monthly, then 6-monthly); same height/weight schedule plus **BP**/**HR** (not LFTs) for **atomoxetine**.

Drug-class summary: Stimulants (1st line) — largest/fastest effect, calm comorbid aggression/**ODD**, adverse effects include appetite/weight loss, sleep disturbance, tics, mild growth slowing, rare hallucinations (skin-crawling/visions). **Atomoxetine** — continuous duration, little insomnia, no tic side-effect, may help comorbid depression; slower full effect than stimulants. TCAs — treat **ADHD** plus comorbid depression/anxiety, require **ECG** monitoring (cardiac conduction block risk). Alpha-2 agonists — help non-responders and comorbid tics/aggression, risk of hypertensive rebound if dose missed. Antipsychotics — last resort, least specific, more **EPSE**/metabolic risk.

blocks.text: **CD** requires behaviours from ≥1 of: physical aggression/cruelty, destruction of property, theft/deceit, or frequent serious rule violations. **ICD-10** requires ≥1 behaviour for ≥6 months; **DSM-5** requires ≥3 of 15 behaviours beginning before age 13 for ≥12 months, plus a 'limited prosocial emotions' specifier and childhood-onset (<10y) vs adolescent-onset (>10y) subtypes. **ODD** is a **CD** subtype in **ICD-10** but **DSM-5** excludes an **ODD** diagnosis if **CD** is present.
Isle of Wight study: **CD** was the most common psychiatric disorder among 10–11 year olds. **UK** prevalence 5–7%; male:female ratio 4:1.

Ontario Child Health Survey (1987) top-3 **CD** risk factors: family dysfunction, parental mental illness, low income. Rutter (1978): low socioeconomic status/family income, paternal criminality, overcrowding, maternal neurosis, institutional care, chronic marital discord.

Biological risk factors: genetic clustering (shared heritable susceptibility to **CD**/**ODD**/**ADHD** externalizing disorders); 'callous-unemotional' temperament; low **CSF** serotonin/deficient serotonergic activity in early-onset, more aggressive cases; autonomic under-arousal (low resting heart rate, low electrodermal activity — predicts later aggression); low salivary cortisol; low **IQ** (performance > verbal **IQ**); reduced prefrontal volumes.

Outcome (Moffitt 2002): <50% of **CD** children have persistent severe antisocial problems as adults (Zoccolillo 1992), but **CD** predicts adult criminality/**ASPD**, education/work/finance difficulties, homelessness, substance dependence, poor physical health, and suicidal behaviour.

blocks.text: **NICE**: group-based parent training/education programmes should be the mainstay of treatment for **ODD**/**CD** in children ≤12 years. Functional family therapy (target age 11–18, 8–12 one-hour home sessions over ~3 months; 4 phases: engagement, motivation, behavioural change, generalisation) cuts reoffending by ~50%. Multisystemic therapy (small caseloads of 4–6, 24h availability, ~3-month course, assessment across home/school/peer systems, weekly supervision/quality control) also roughly halves reoffending and reduces inpatient time.

**ODD**: enduring pattern of negative/hostile/defiant behaviour without **CD**-level rights violations, ≥6 months. Almost invariably present at home first (may or may not extend to school/peers). Onset as early as age 3, typically noted by age 8, rarely later than adolescence; onset generally earlier than **CD**. Prevalence 2–5%; more common in boys pre-puberty, equal sex ratio post-puberty. 25% show no later symptoms, but many progress to **CD**.

Conduct disorder is thought to have the **LEAST** genetic loading of common childhood psychiatric conditions (contrast with **ADHD**'s highest heritability) — though twin/adoption studies still show conduct problems are substantially heritable.

sections.title: 5. Childhood & Adolescent Depression, Suicide & Deliberate Self-Harm

blocks.text: Pre-puberty depression prevalence ~1%, no sex difference; post-puberty ~3%, commoner in females. 50% remain clinically depressed at 12 months, but most recover within 2 years. Adolescent depression shows continuity into adulthood (~30% recurrence within 5 years). The full pure syndrome is rare before puberty; formal operational thought in early adolescence permits experienced hopelessness akin to adult depression.

Clinical features by age: young children — poor feeding, failure to thrive, tantrums, irritability, separation anxiety, hyperactivity, regressed behaviour (enuresis/soiling). Older children — somatisation (headache/abdominal/chest pain), hypochondriacal ideas, school refusal, declining schoolwork. Adolescents — environment-influenced low mood, anhedonia/social withdrawal (powerful indicators), low self-esteem, biological symptoms, suicidal acts, behavioural problems, substance abuse.

95% of major depression in young people occurs against longstanding psychosocial difficulty. Comorbidity is the rule (50–80%): anxiety 50–80% (often precedes depression), conduct disorder 25%, **OCD** 15%, eating disorder 5%; **ADHD** and depression may be co-transmitted in families.

**NICE** stepped care: mild — 2 weeks watchful waiting, then supportive therapy/self-help/group **CBT**. Moderate–severe — **CAMHS** review, ±3 months individual **CBT**/**IPT**/brief family therapy; combination treatment (psychotherapy + medication) should be considered in **ALL** cases. Psychotherapy is recommended **BEFORE** pharmacotherapy for moderate-severe depression.

**Fluoxetine** is first-line (**NICE**), **sertraline**/**citalopram** second-line — **fluoxetine** is the best-studied, with **FDA**/**MHRA** approval and **CSM** allowance for use in children/adolescents. **Paroxetine** shows little benefit and more adverse effects/discontinuation/suicidal-behaviour risk. TCAs unsupported by trials and cardiotoxic. Monitor for agitation/irritability/behaviour change/suicidality at initiation and dose changes.

**TADS** (n=439): **CBT** alone (43% improved) was **NOT** superior to placebo (35%); combination **CBT**+**fluoxetine** (71%) and **fluoxetine** alone (61%) were both markedly superior to **CBT** and placebo. Combination beat **fluoxetine** alone on remission (37% vs 20%). **ECT** is not recommended for ages 5–11; in older patients, reserved for severe/life-threatening/treatment-refractory depression.

Suicide is the 3rd leading cause of adolescent death (accidents, homicide, then suicide); males complete suicide more than females at all ages/cultures, but suicidal ideation (14% boys, 25% girls) and attempts/**DSH** are more common in females. Self-poisoning is the commonest parasuicide method (analgesics/psychotropics); hanging is commonest in boys who complete suicide, overdose/jumping from height in girls who complete suicide. 10% of adolescent attempters repeat within a year; 40% of completers had a previous attempt.

blocks.text: Paediatric mania typically presents atypically/with mixed features: irritability, labile mood, behavioural problems (rather than classic euphoria). Elated mood and irritability show the most cross-study variability. Prevalence in adolescents ~1% (up to 6% including subsyndromal symptoms); M>F in childhood, M=F in adolescence. Up to 60% of adults with bipolar disorder retrospectively report onset before age 20.

Comorbidity in paediatric **BPAD**: ~70% **ADHD**, 40% **ODD**, 30% anxiety disorder, 40% substance misuse, 8% Tourette's, 3% bulimia nervosa. Depressive episodes with psychomotor/psychotic features, or a family history of mania, or hypomania/mania triggered by antidepressants, predict later conversion from depression to mania.

Early-onset **BPAD** prognosis is poor (~50% long-term functional decline), often chronic with atypical/rapid-cycling features; completed-suicide rate ~10%. **NICE**: use adult medication guidelines at lower doses. Atypical antipsychotics (**olanzapine**, **risperidone**) preferred first-line for acute mania, followed by **valproate**/**lithium**; avoid **valproate** in girls/young women (**PCOS**/infertility risk). Higher **lithium** mg/kg doses may be needed in children (higher renal filtration, more body water) to reach 0.4–1.0 mEq/L; neurological side effects (tremor, drowsiness, ataxia, confusion) may be more prominent.

Childhood-onset schizophrenia (**COS**): onset by age 12; early-onset schizophrenia (**EOS**) = onset before 18; very-early-onset (**VEOS**) = before 13. Prepubertal schizophrenia is exceedingly rare; adolescent prevalence is ~50x that of younger children (1–2/1000). Slight male preponderance, more marked (2:1) in **VEOS**. **COS** shows more negative symptoms, disorganisation, fewer systematised/persecutory delusions, and a more chronic course with less full recovery than adult-onset.

**COS** premorbid course: greater delays in language, reading, bladder control, social functioning than adult-onset; neuropsychological deficits in attention/working memory/premorbid **IQ**. Genetic risk 5–10% in first-degree relatives (vs 0.2–0.6% controls); heritability up to 82%; cytogenetic abnormalities more common than in adult-onset. **MRI** shows enlarged lateral ventricles and grey-matter loss progressing from parietal to frontal/temporal regions (more than adult-onset).

Risk of premature death in **COS** is higher than adult-onset schizophrenia (8.5% in a 106-case study); risk of suicide/accidental death from psychosis ~5% (vs adult schizophrenia suicide rate of 10%). Treatment mirrors adult algorithms; atypicals favoured, more intensive metabolic monitoring needed; typicals (e.g. **haloperidol**) carry more **EPSE** risk in young people (acute dystonia more common, akathisia less common than in adults); avoid depot/sedating antipsychotics; **clozapine** effective in treatment-resistant adolescent psychosis but with higher neutropenia/seizure risk than adults.

**Aripiprazole** and **lithium** are the only medications licensed for treating paediatric mania; in practice, **NICE** (2020 update) recommends **aripiprazole** or an alternative antipsychotic (**risperidone**, **olanzapine**, **quetiapine**) for acute manic/mixed episodes, limiting drug treatment to 12 weeks — **valproate** monotherapy should **NOT** be first-line, and should **NOT** be offered to girls/young women of childbearing potential (teratogenicity, **PCOS** risk).

sections.title: 7. Anxiety Disorders in Children — General Features & Separation Anxiety

blocks.text: Anxiety disorder diagnosis requires the 'impairment criterion' — significant interference in everyday functioning, not just distress that is extreme relative to peers. Overall prevalence 5–15% (8% needing clinical treatment). Equal M:F in childhood; F:M ~2:1 after adolescence.

Prevalence by disorder: separation anxiety disorder 3.5% (children), 0.8% (adolescents); **GAD** ~4% of adolescents; specific phobia ~10% (2x commoner in females); social phobia 1% (children), 5–15% (adolescents); panic disorder 3–6%, peak onset 15–19 years.

Age-related presentation: tearfulness/clinging in preschoolers; somatic complaints/hypochondriacal fretting/irritability/aggression in middle childhood (5–12y); **SAD** and specific phobia typically onset in early childhood; **GAD** occurs across all ages; **OCD**, social phobia and panic disorder tend to arise in later childhood/adolescence.

Comorbidity patterns: **SAD** more often comorbid with specific phobia than **GAD**/social phobia are; **GAD**/social phobia more often comorbid with mood disorders than **SAD** is. Up to 90% of young people with **GAD** have a comorbid diagnosis. Depression is 8.2x as likely in anxious children; the **GAD**–depression link persists into adulthood.

Separation anxiety disorder: excessive, developmentally inappropriate worry about separation from an attachment figure — sleep disturbance/nightmares about separation, somatisation (nausea, headache, stomach ache), and school refusal are the commonest presenting complaints. Duration ≥4 weeks; onset before age 18 (labelled 'early onset' if before age 6).

blocks.text: Romanian Adoptees Study: children removed from severely deprived institutions and adopted in Canada/**UK** — 20% had severe attachment disturbances by age 6; duration of deprivation exposure strongly predicted severe disinhibited behaviour.

Reactive attachment disorder: persistent abnormal social-relationship pattern with emotional disturbance, reactive to environmental change; diagnosed before age 5; inhibited or disinhibited subtypes; commoner in poverty/social disruption. Caused by severe parental neglect/abuse/mishandling (also: young, isolated, inexperienced, or depressed caretaker). Features: fearfulness/hypervigilance not responsive to comforting, poor peer interaction, aggression to self/others, sometimes growth failure.

Disinhibited attachment disorder: abnormal social functioning arising in the first 5 years — early clinging/diffuse non-selective attachment behaviour, replaced by age 4 with attention-seeking and indiscriminately friendly behaviour, which may persist into middle/later childhood with associated emotional/behavioural disturbance.

Sibling rivalry disorder: onset within 6 months of a younger sibling's birth; duration ≥4 weeks; abnormal-degree emotional disturbance (anxiety, regression, tantrums, dysphoria, sleep difficulty, oppositional/attention-seeking behaviour — ≥2 features required); behaviour ranges from reluctance to share up to overt hostility/physical harm toward the sibling (**ICD-10**).

Reactive attachment disorder cannot be diagnosed before age 1 (or developmental age <9 months, before selective attachment capacity is established) or in the context of autism spectrum disorder — even when an adequate primary caregiver becomes newly available, the child does not turn to them for comfort/support and rarely shows security-seeking behaviour.

sections.title: 9. School Refusal vs Truancy, and Selective Mutism

blocks.text: School refusal is a problem, not a diagnosis; it co-occurs with anxiety/depressive disorders. Three incidence peaks: age 5–7 (school entry, possible separation anxiety), age 11 (commonest presentation age, transition to secondary school), and age 14+ (possibly first presentation of depression/anxiety, or bullying/exam pressure). Incidence 1–5%, sex distribution equal. 70% successfully reintegrate; social anxiety/communication problems may persist in the rest.

blocks.text: Selective mutism: persistent failure to speak in specific settings (e.g. school) despite full language use at home; onset usually age 3–5, after normal speech acquisition; rare (3–8/10,000 **UK**); slightly more common in girls; high rate of associated psychiatric disorder, especially social phobia. No treatment shown generally effective; behavioural approach with positive reinforcement is helpful.

Anxiety-disorder key-characteristics summary (Lewis's Child & Adolescent Psychiatry): **SAD** is a possible risk factor for adult panic disorder/agoraphobia; social phobia has behavioural inhibition as a temperamental predictor; **GAD** requires ≥1 somatic complaint and has a close genetic link with depression; specific phobia has 5 types, some corresponding to evolutionary dangers (snakes, blood); panic disorder/agoraphobia can be mimicked by medical conditions (hyperthyroidism, cardiac abnormalities).

Treatment of childhood anxiety: **CBT** (relaxation training, cognitive restructuring) is effective; individual **CBT** + family component may add benefit, particularly for girls; group **CBT** effective for social phobia. SSRIs are first-line pharmacological agents (good efficacy/safety data for social phobia, **SAD**, **GAD**). Benzodiazepines are **NOT** routinely indicated; little evidence for **buspirone** or beta-blockers.
The commonest age of presentation for school refusal is 11 years (peak 11–13), coinciding with the transition to secondary school; incidence 1–5% with equal sex distribution.

blocks.text: **PTSD** occurs frequently in children/adolescents — up to 6% meet criteria at some point; **UK** National Survey of Mental Health found 0.4% of 11–15 year olds diagnosed, with girls at twice the rate of boys. Common exposures: physical/sexual abuse (can be chronic), domestic/school/community violence, kidnapping, terrorism, accidents, disasters.

**DSM-5** lowers the diagnostic threshold for children and adds a separate criterion set for children under age 6. Trauma classification: Type 1 — single acute event (commonest in children); symptoms include full detailed memories, 'omens'/cognitive reappraisal, misperceptions. Type 2 — longstanding/repeated exposure (e.g. chronic abuse); symptoms include denial, psychic numbing, self-hypnosis, depersonalisation, dissociation, rage, self-harm, extreme passivity.

Trauma-focused **CBT** (8–12 sessions, evidence from several RCTs) is the mainstay treatment; single-session psychological debriefing is **NOT** supported by evidence. **NICE**: medications should **NOT** be routinely prescribed for children/young people with **PTSD**, despite SSRIs (e.g. **citalopram** 20–40mg over 8 weeks, open trial) being frequently used off-label. **EMDR** has no controlled trial evidence (one inconclusive unpublished trial). No good evidence for play therapy, art therapy, or family therapy alone.

Within 1 month of a traumatic event, consider active monitoring or individual trauma-focused **CBT**. >1 month post-trauma, trauma-focused **CBT** is the treatment of choice. Consider **EMDR** for ages 7–17 presenting >3 months post-trauma only if they don't respond to/engage with **CBT**. Do **NOT** use psychological debriefing or drug treatments for **PTSD** prevention/treatment under 18.

blocks.text: Characteristic childhood **PTSD** features include compulsive repetitive play re-enacting the trauma (without relieving anxiety), intrusive re-experiencing/flashbacks, avoidance, nightmares, developmental regression (language, toileting), hyperarousal/hypervigilance, decreased concentration, new separation anxiety and new aggression — selective amnesia for the event is **NOT** a characteristic feature.

sections.title: 11. OCD in Children, PANDAS & Sydenham's Chorea

blocks.text: Childhood **OCD** is characterised by secrecy — children understand their behaviour is unusual and try to hide it. 40% of affected children lack obsessive thoughts; rituals/habits occur in 2/3 but are less frequent/intense and less distressing than adult **OCD**. Prevalence ~0.5%; onset as early as age 5 (mean onset age 10); childhood-onset ratio 2 boys:1 girl, but post-pubertal onset is more common in girls.

Aetiology: increased incidence in 1st-degree relatives and **MZ** twins (80% vs 40% **DZ** — note: source text states this **MZ** figure while comparing to itself, reflecting the original text's phrasing); possible autoimmune process; reduced caudate nucleus volume; hyperactive orbitofrontal circuits (**SPET**); 5-**HT** receptor dysfunction (**SSRI** response); dopaminergic dysfunction (high-dose stimulants can worsen **OCD** symptoms).

Comorbidity: 70% have ≥1 comorbid disorder — tic disorders 17–40%, major depression 26%, specific developmental disabilities 24%, plus higher-than-expected **ADHD**, **ASD** and Tourette's rates. **DSM-IV** allows **OCD** diagnosis alongside schizophrenia.

Paediatric **OCD** Treatment Study (**POTS**): combination of **sertraline** + **CBT** was superior to either alone. **Fluoxetine** and **sertraline** are licensed for childhood/adolescent **OCD** (per **BNF**/**NICE** guidance in the book text); **fluoxetine** specifically recommended when significant comorbid depression is present. **Clomipramine** is **NOT** recommended first-line (hypotension/arrhythmia/seizure risk vs SSRIs).

Treatment ladder: mild impairment — self-help guides first; mild-moderate impairment not responding — **CBT** (including exposure-response prevention); severe impairment or inadequate response — add **SSRI** to psychotherapy. Most guidelines recommend a **CBT** trial before medication, though **POTS** evidence favours combined **SSRI**+**CBT** as optimal.

**PANDAS**: **OCD**/tic symptoms associated with beta-haemolytic streptococcal infection — believed to signify an autoimmune process akin to Sydenham's chorea in rheumatic fever. Pre-pubertal onset common; episodic/'sawtooth' course; choreiform movements. 75% of children with Sydenham's chorea also have **OCD** symptoms. >50% of tic-disorder clinic patients report abrupt onset/exacerbation with infection (11% within 6 months of streptococcal infection, per Singer et al). Hypothesised mechanism: strep exposure triggers immune activation → basal ganglia inflammation → disrupted cortico-striatal-thalamo-cortical function; basal ganglia volume correlates with **OCD**/**PANDAS** severity on **MRI**.

blocks.text: Primary nocturnal enuresis: strongest predictor is a family history of enuresis (70% have an affected parent/sibling); reduced renal sensitivity to vasopressin (antidiuretic effect) also implicated. Secondary enuresis: predicted by delayed bedwetting control and high rate of adverse life events; daytime enuresis more linked to structural abnormalities; sexual abuse is associated with secondary wetting.

Rule out organic causes before diagnosing enuresis: **UTI**, obstruction, genitourinary pathology, spina bifida occulta, diabetes mellitus/insipidus. Associated with stressful life events, low **SES**, large/overcrowded families; often self-limited; comorbid encopresis and **ADHD** are more likely in these children.

Treatment: first review appropriate toilet training; psychoeducation (avoid punishment); behavioural interventions (bell-and-pad/enuresis alarm — classical conditioning, most effective treatment, >60% achieve dryness); star charts. Medications: **imipramine** (short-term use, approved); desmopressin (intranasal, adverse effects include headache/nasal congestion/epistaxis/stomachache, one reported case of hyponatraemic convulsion); **reboxetine** investigated as a safer non-cardiotoxic alternative to **imipramine**; oxybutynin (anticholinergic, increases bladder capacity, rarely used).

Encopresis: voiding/soiling of formed stools inappropriately at mental age ≥4 years, ≥once/month for ≥6 months, absent sufficient organic cause. Males 6x more likely than females; ~5% of children over age 4 affected. >75% show evidence of chronic constipation → impaction → overflow soiling, though organic causes (Hirschsprung's disease, anorectal pathology, neurological/nutritional disorders, drug side effects) must be excluded — Hirschsprung's disease is the chief differential to exclude.

Hirschsprung's disease is specifically the disorder to exclude as the chief organic differential in encopresis (empty rectum, no urge to defecate, but overflow soiling can still occur) — a recurring named-differential recall trap.

blocks.text: Encopresis is linked with sexual abuse history (possible defence against further abuse, or pain-related retention), maternal hostility, and harsh/punitive parenting. Treatment: paediatric assessment/imaging if indicated, evacuate retained stool, laxatives, family psychoeducation/non-punitive atmosphere, behavioural operant training with positive reinforcement; biofeedback adds nothing to laxative treatment (**RCT** evidence). Usually self-limited; most soiling stops by age 16.

Pica: persistent (>1 month) eating of non-nutritive substances at developmentally inappropriate age (>1 year), ≥twice weekly; typically 2nd–3rd year of life; common in intellectual disability. Consequences: toxicity, infection, **GIT** ulceration/obstruction. Hypothesised causes: hunger, malnutrition, nutritional deficiency, psychosocial stress, hypothalamic lesions.

**ICD-11** defines enuresis as repeated voiding of urine into clothes/bed (day or night) at/after the developmental age when continence is ordinarily expected (5 years); nocturnal enuresis is commoner in males, diurnal enuresis commoner in females; a child's enuresis risk is >7x higher if the father was enuretic.

blocks.text: Childhood autism (Kanner's autism): triad of qualitative social-interaction impairment, communication impairment (language delay is the commonest referral trigger), and restricted/repetitive behaviour/interests; 'lack of theory of mind' is characteristic. Onset before age 3 by definition (sometimes not diagnosed until much later). 4x more frequent in boys; prevalence has apparently risen over time.

Genetics: sibling recurrence rate 2–8%; risk in a sibling of 2 affected children 25–30%; overall heritability ~90%. Twin concordance **MZ** 36% vs **DZ** 0% in one study, ~96% vs 27% in another. Chromosomes 2, 4, 7, 13, 15, 19 (and weaker signals at 16, 17) implicated; **NRXN1**/**NLGN3** genes implicated. Associated with Fragile X syndrome (~1–4% of autism cases) and tuberous sclerosis (up to 2%), also congenital rubella and phenylketonuria.

~10% of autistic children have an identifiable medical condition; ~80% of autism cases have learning disability (about 1/3 mild-moderate); by contrast, ~80% of people with autism spectrum disorders more broadly have intellectual abilities within the normal range. **MRI**: larger brain volumes/early accelerated growth, enlarged lateral/4th ventricles, frontal/cerebellar abnormalities (vermal lobule **VI**/**VII** hypoplasia), greatest volume increase in occipital/parietal/temporal lobes (not frontal). Cerebellar pathology includes fewer Purkinje cells.

~1/3 of autistic patients have high plasma serotonin; high **CSF** homovanillic acid associates with withdrawal/stereotypies in some. Congenital rubella (especially 1st-trimester exposure) is associated; obstetric complications are **NOT** currently thought causal; child-rearing practices do **NOT** cause autism; the **MMR**-autism link arose from a single flawed study, not replicated elsewhere.

Autism is a lifelong neurodevelopmental disorder. Good prognosis predictors: communicative speech by age 6, **IQ** >50, employment-consistent skill. ≥60% will be unable to live independently. Long-term outcome: 12% very good, 10% good, 19% fair, 46% poor, 12% very poor; communication/reading/spelling impaired in most; stereotypies/restricted interests persist in most.

No cure exists. Applied Behavioural Analysis (40h/week for 3 years, operant conditioning/imitation/reinforcement) and **TEACCH** (based on belief children are motivated to learn language; reduces self-injury, enhances life skills) are the two named specific programmes. **CBT** can be difficult due to literal understanding/rigid thinking. SSRIs used for repetitive behaviours (limited evidence, lower doses than antidepressant dosing). Second-generation antipsychotics are first-line pharmacotherapy for **ASD** with associated irritability/aggression — **risperidone** is the only medication licensed in the **UK** for this indication (monitor weight gain, somnolence, hyperglycaemia). **Melatonin** shown beneficial for sleep latency/efficiency in several small studies.
Preterm birth is associated with a considerably higher-than-general-population prevalence of autism spectrum disorder.

sections.title: 14. Asperger's Syndrome, Rett's Syndrome & Childhood Disintegrative Disorder

blocks.text: Asperger's syndrome: same qualitative social-interaction abnormalities and restricted/stereotyped behaviour/interests as autism, but **IQ** and language are usually normal, with **NO** significant delay in language, cognitive development, or age-appropriate self-help skills (unlike autism). Mild motor clumsiness and family history of autism may be present. Global prevalence ~6/10,000 (about 1/3 as common as autism). Good prognosis linked to normal **IQ** and high-level social skills. High psychiatric comorbidity — depression is commonest; **BPAD** and schizophrenia are more common than in the general population.

Rett's syndrome: rare X-linked dominant disorder (MeCP2 gene mutation), almost exclusively affects females. Normal head circumference/milestones at birth; head growth decelerates between 6–18 months producing microcephaly; loss of purposeful hand movements (replaced by stereotypies e.g. hand-wringing, licking/biting fingers, tapping/slapping); loss of previously acquired speech; psychomotor retardation and ataxic/apraxic gait. Seizures in up to 75%; disorganised **EEG** in almost all (even without clinical seizures); irregular respiration (hyperventilation, apnoea, breath-holding, normalising in sleep). Scoliosis/spasticity common. Developmental arrest plateaus; many reach adulthood with major disability and poor prognosis.

expansion: Deceleration of speech + purposeful hand movements, replaced by stereotypies (hand-wringing)

blocks.text: Childhood disintegrative disorder (Heller's disease/disintegrative psychosis): marked regression across several functional domains after ≥2 years of apparently normal development, with loss of acquired motor/language/social skills between ages 3–4. Diagnosis requires loss of skills in ≥2 of: language, social/adaptive behaviour, bowel/bladder control, play, motor skills; plus abnormalities in ≥2 of: reciprocal social interaction, communication, stereotyped/restricted behaviour. Stereotypies/compulsions common; main neurological association is seizure disorder; male predominance; cause unknown; prognosis poor (most left with ≥moderate intellectual disability).

The most common psychiatric comorbidity in Asperger's syndrome is depression; the male:female ratio for diagnosed Asperger's is 9:1 (partly reflecting a referral bias, with boys referred ~9x more often — Wagner 2006).

blocks.text: Reading disorder (dyslexia): impaired word recognition, slow/inaccurate reading, poor comprehension, phonological-processing deficit; identifiable by age 7; affects 4% of school-age children; male predominance 4:1; often familial; ~20% comorbid **CD**/**ADHD** (conversely 15–30% of **ADHD** children have a learning disorder). Assessment tools: **WORD**, **TOWRE**, **WISC**.

Disorder of written expression: spelling/grammar/punctuation/paragraph-organisation/handwriting difficulties; often coexists with dyslexia; occurs in 2–8% of school-age children with 3:1 male predominance; **ADHD** more frequent in this group.

Mathematics disorder: up to 6% of school-age children affected, reported **MORE** commonly in **FEMALES** (unlike the other learning disorders' male predominance); often linked to visuospatial deficits/right parietal dysfunction; difficulty with number names, arithmetic signs, multiplication tables, word-problem translation, calculation speed.

Expressive language disorder: selective expressive deficit relative to receptive language/nonverbal intelligence; prevalence 3–5%; 2–3x commoner in boys; familial. Mixed receptive-expressive language disorder: both comprehension and expression impaired, expressive component often more severe than pure expressive disorder; persists in ~3% of school-age children, ~2x commoner in boys.

Phonological disorder: delayed/incapable production of age-expected speech sounds (omissions, substitutions, distortions), not due to physical/dysarthric causes; recognisable from early childhood, often by age 3 in severe cases.

Stuttering: disrupted speech flow (repetitions, prolongations, dysrhythmic phonation, blocking); struggles with initial syllables; male predominance 3:1; prevalence ~1%; typical onset age 2–7 (peak age 5); 50–80% (mostly mild cases) recover spontaneously; **NOT** normally associated with a psychiatric disorder itself, though preschool/school-age stutterers show increased social anxiety and school refusal, and adolescent persistence raises social-isolation rates. Aetiology: genetic, incomplete cerebral dominance, hyperdopaminergic state. Management: speech therapy.
Reading difficulties affect approximately 5% (4–7%) of children in Britain — developmental dyslexia is common in the English-speaking developed world at this rate.

blocks.text: Tourette syndrome: multiple motor + ≥1 vocal tic, present ≥1 year, causing distress/impairment, occurring many times daily in bouts, with never a tic-free period >3 consecutive months. Vocal tics begin 1–2 years after motor tics, ranging from meaningless sounds to words (barks/hisses/hoots), and may include coprolalia (~1/3, mostly not in children), echolalia/echopraxia (~10%), palilalia. Tics wax/wane, exacerbated by stress/anxiety/fatigue. Onset before age 18, mean onset age 7; prevalence ~1% in children; 3–4x more common in males; **MZ** twin concordance 50% vs **DZ** 10%.

Aetiology: autosomal dominant/polygenic pattern (increased **MZ** twin/1st-degree relative concordance); overlap with **OCD** genetic liability; functional dopamine excess implicated (antipsychotics reduce symptoms); **clonidine**'s effectiveness implicates noradrenaline; basal ganglia/premotor/motor cortex circuits on neuroimaging. Post-infectious autoimmune mechanism: **GABHS** infection odds ratio 3.1 in preceding 3 months for new-onset **TS**, rising to **OR** 12.1 with multiple **GABHS** infections in the preceding year (dose-dependent); significant association also with new **OCD**/tic diagnoses.

Comorbidity: **OCD** in 1/3–2/3 of children/adolescents with Tourette's (1/3 of affected adults retain **OCD** into adulthood); **ADHD** up to 50%; also depression, anxiety, impulse-control and conduct problems — more prevalent than chance association alone would predict.

Management: psychoeducation first for individual/family/schools. **CBT** techniques (if exposure-response prevention achievable) can help tics and **OCD** symptoms: relaxation, exposure-response prevention, massed practice, habit reversal. Medication reserved for disabling/refractory tics: **clonidine** (α2-agonist) tried **FIRST** — reduces tic severity/frequency, main side effects sedation/postural hypotension; **guanfacine** (α2-agonist) shows ~30% reduction in tic ratings with more acceptable side effects. Antipsychotics (**haloperidol**, pimozide, **sulpiride**, **risperidone**) are effective but side-effect burden may outweigh benefit, so are **NOT** first-line despite superiority to placebo in small RCTs.

Transient tic disorder: single/multiple motor and/or vocal tics, many times/day, nearly every day for ≥4 weeks but ≤12 consecutive months; onset before age 18; criteria never met for Tourette's/chronic tic disorder; occurs in 5–20% of children, 80% outgrown by adulthood.

Chronic tic disorder: persists >1 year with relapses/remissions; motor **OR** vocal tics but **NOT** both simultaneously (a form of 'partial Tourette syndrome'); one tic form may fade and be replaced by another over time; rarer than the transient form.

blocks.text: Alcohol is the most commonly abused substance by adolescents (~30% of 13-year-olds report weekly use); binge-drinking pattern is more common than other abuse patterns. Cigarette smoking is decreasing in the West due to legislation/changing perception. Cannabis: ~5% of **UK** 11–16 year olds have tried it, rising significantly in late teens.

Heroin use under-18 has increased in the **UK**/many countries in the past decade; ≥15% of users switch to **IV** use within a year. Cocaine: 2.4% of **US** 12–17 year olds have used it (lifetime), vs 0.5% of **UK** 11–15 year olds. Party drugs (**MDMA**, **GHB**, **ketamine**, rohypnol) are a small proportion of adolescent substance problems but increasingly tried at younger ages. Methamphetamine lifetime use fell from 4.7% (1999) to 2.5% (2005). **US** anabolic steroid use: 4–12% of male adolescents (no reliable **UK** data, likely lower). **LSD**/hallucinogen use is down from a 1990s peak.
No known effective pharmacotherapy exists for adolescent inhalant abuse; first-line treatment is multimodal — individual **CBT**, family therapy, and activity/engagement programmes.

sections.title: 18. Rating Scales & Assessment Tools in Child Psychiatry

blocks.text: Connor's questionnaire: obtains **ADHD**-symptom information from parents/schoolteachers (also parent/adolescent versions). **ADI-R** (Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised): 93-item structured research interview covering language/communication, reciprocal social interaction, restricted/stereotyped behaviour — used for formal diagnosis and educational planning. **WISC**: verbal + performance subscales yielding verbal/performance/full-scale **IQ**, for children <16 years (**WAIS** is the adult equivalent).

**SDQ** (Strengths & Difficulties Questionnaire): generic screen for emotional/behavioural/prosocial problems, validated ages 4–16, quick to complete. **CBCL** (Child Behavior Checklist): 113-item Likert parent/teacher-rated scale for children 4–16, useful when symptoms differ across settings, mainly used in **ODD**/**CD**. **CAFAS** (Child & Adolescent Functional Assessment Scale): clinician-rated functional-impairment measure, ages 7–17, ~10 minutes. Children's Depression Inventory: depression severity, ages 7–17. Beck Depression Inventory: usable for screening only from age 14. **CY-BOCS**: paediatric version of Y-**BOCS** for childhood **OCD** severity.

Psychiatric hospitalisation is generally not preferred in child/adolescent psychiatry given disruption to normal developmental context. Hersov's (1994) admission criteria: (1) diagnostic work not achievable as outpatient, (2) severe disorder needing multiprofessional inpatient care, (3) impaired physical status needing skilled nursing; and criteria justifying removal from home: (4) adverse home/family circumstances precluding improvement, (5) gross parental overprotection after trauma precluding recovery.

The Clinical Interview Schedule-Revised (**CIS-R**) can be used to assign **ICD** diagnoses and is suitable for re-administration at a later age (e.g. following up a 14-year-old again at age 20), making it useful for longitudinal symptom tracking across the child-to-adult transition.
